text: Run Lesson 54's pipeline enough nights in a row, and eventually something genuinely breaks — a brief network blip, a server mid-restart during a patch window. Right now, that pipeline run simply fails: no retry, no notification, no record of what actually happened beyond a red status the next morning. That's not acceptable for something running unattended at three AM.

The cheapest fix goes directly on the activity itself. A brief network blip or a server finishing its restart thirty seconds late now gets silently absorbed — three retries, a minute apart, before the activity is even considered failed. Most of Northwind's real 3 AM problems are exactly this transient.

Retries handle transient failures. For a real, sustained failure — the SQL Server actually down for the night — the pipeline needs a genuine error-handling pattern. LogFailureToTable runs a stored procedure recording the failure into a monitoring table. Because this is Try-Catch, not Do-If-Else, a handled failure still lets the pipeline complete without erroring the whole run, while leaving a real audit trail.

Some failures are too serious to just log and move past — Northwind losing an entire night's sales data is exactly one of them. A failed activity runs metric, scoped specifically to this one Copy activity, backed by an action group that emails the on-call engineer immediately. This is the layer that actually wakes someone up — deliberately the last resort.

Three real layers, one shared principle: each only escalates to the next when the one before it genuinely couldn't handle the problem. Retry, silent. Try-Catch-Proceed, silent but recorded. Alert, human, deliberately, only at the end.

A pipeline that now survives its own bad nights, on its own, with a real record when it doesn't. Next: Build the Mapping Data Flow — turning those raw sales rows into exactly what the eight AM meeting actually needs to see.
